title: I like 'em thick: an apology to my English teachers
titleZh: 我喜欢厚厚的：向我的英语老师道歉
author: Ariarule
relevanceReason: 命中 2 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: photo cred: my dadI owe an apology to every English teacher I ever had. I always assumed that so-called “great” literature was a hoax, a punishment inflicted upon adolescents for the crime of being young. These books did not have anything special about them, and covering up that fact was simply a make-work exercise for former English majors, a sort of “jobs for snobs” program.I was wrong about this. There is such thing as greatness. More specifically, there is such thing as thickness. Great works of fiction—for that matter, great works of any art—unfurl in response to your attention. The more time you spend with them, the more you get out of them. That kind of responsiveness is so addicting that it can lead people to do crazy things, like try to teach literature to high schoolers.But thickness is tricky, because rewarding the careful reader often means repelling the casual one. And this is where I would like an apology in return from my English teachers, because while this might have been obvious to them, they never made it obvious to me.I was presented with art and literature as if it was self-explanatory, and that everything wonderful about it was plainly visible from the outside. But those works were much more like dark, winding caves with treasure stashed inside of them. My teachers were like, “Right, well, into the cave you go!” and I was like “But there’s nothing in there” and they were like “Entering the cave is 30% of your grade” and so I took a few steps into the darkness and I was like “Just as I suspected: an empty cave” and then I came trudging back out and pretended that I saw something.But if someone had outfitted me appropriately, if they warned me that you have to bring one of those crank-up flashlights and you might have to shimmy through some narrow antechambers and spelunk through some flooded passageways, but that eventually you would reach a room full of untold riches—well, maybe I would have actually tried.Instead, I had to learn about thickness by looking at a guy’s butt.For most of my life, I treated art museums like celebrity scavenger hunts. The point of visiting was to see in person the thing you had seen on a screen or in a book; the goal was collection rather than contemplation. And so I would power-walk through the galleries, scanning the placards for famous names, rushing over whenever one of my companions would hiss, “Oh, this one’s a Van Gogh!”This ended when I encountered The Garden of Earthly Delights, a triptych painted by the Dutch master Hieronymous Bosch. When I went to collect that one, I got stuck. I wanted to stand in front of it forever.It’s a painting from 500 years in the past that looks like a painting from 500 years in the future. Every corner of it is filled with “freakish riddles” and “irresponsible phantasmagoria”, in the words of art critic Wilhelm Fränger. For example, what is going on with this dude?Or this lil guy here?In the third panel of the triptych, there’s a scene of some instruments, some naked dudes, and some kind of pink demon with an alarmingly long tongue. Look closely, and you’ll see one of the naked dudes has some music printed on his butt (helpfully, one of his friends is pointing at it, as if to say, “dude you have some music on your butt”).In 2012, a student at Oklahoma Christian University named Amelia Hamrick noticed the butt music and decided to transcribe it, record it, and post it to her blog, catapulting her to instant worldwide fame.When I started writing this section, I intended to include this fact as a fun little Easter egg—look how thick this painting is, that it goes to the trouble of writing an actual song on a guy’s hiney!But it turns out I got this all wrong, and the painting was even thicker than I thought. While researching the story, I stumbled upon three magisterial blog posts by Ian Pittman, an expert on medieval music. He argues:Hamrick was not the first to resurrect the butt music. It was also done by the Swedish group Vox Vulgaris in 2003, Atrium Musicae in 1978 (from the LP Codex Gluteo), and, according to a now-deleted angry comment, by some art history professors in 1981 and 1961, whose erasure from this story has left them quite, if you will, butthurt.The butt music is not music at all. It lacks a clef, the notes are spaced out randomly, and one of the staffs has a different number of lines. If you try to turn it into a coherent song, you’re basically making things up—or as we would call it if an LLM did it, hallucinating. (Perhaps this is why every rendition of the butt music has sounded so different.)Bosch intended the butt music to be unplayable. If you look across his works, understand the context of his life, and spend a little extra time inspecting The Garden of Earthly Delights, you realize that Bosch thought secular music was a one-way ticket to hell. (Church music was a-ok, as long as it was for the glory of god and not the glory of the players.) That’s why he depicted so many musicians being tortured: one of them is trapped inside a drum that’s being beaten by some kind of raccoon demon, another is being crucified on a harp, and the butt music guy himself is being crushed by a giant lute. For Bosch, putting actual music on a guy’s ass would be like the FBI handing out copies of the Anarchist Cookbook.So the butt music is not a secret, but a warning: “If you play music outside of a church context, demons will torture you for eternity.” I find this funny, because I grew up amidst a moral panic over rap music; just imagine growing up in a moral panic over all music. “Oh, your heart will go on, Celine Dion? No, your heart will be torn from your chest and fed to the slavering servants of Beelzebub.”So that’s what thickness looks like, but what is it? What makes something thick?There is no straightforward answer to this question, which is what makes thickness both rare and remarkable in the first place. But I think there are four thickening agents worth considering:Thick art bears the marks of approaches attempted and discarded, a pile of scraps larger than the finished project. For example, here are four versions of the same idea from the artist Hokusai, one produced when he was 33, another when he was 44, another at 46, and another when he was 72, which is the one you’ll recognize.1The Betty Crocker Corporation could put just egg powder into their cake mix, but they don’t, because cracking an egg into a bowl allows people to pretend that they’re baking. When you present your grandma with a birthday cake, you want to feel like “I made this for you, O Beloved Grandmama” and not like “I dumped a bag of dust into a bowl and heated it up so open wide you old biddy.”Thick art is like that: it gives you an egg to crack. It leaves space for some essential ingredient you bring yourself, so that the real action happens in your mind, rather than on the page or the canvas or the screen.This effect is often too subtle to demonstrate in a single bullet point, but here’s an accessible example. The 11th Hour by Graeme Base reads like a normal children’s book at first—oh look here are some beautiful pictures of animals, look at them playing board games, how nice, etc.Only at the end of the story do you realize that a crime has been taking place under your nose the whole time, and that the clues are hidden in the details of the pictures you’ve just been paging through. The real experience of the book is re-reading the book with this in mind.Why this word, this scene, this character, and not some other one? Thin art has no answers; thick art does. Sometimes these reasons are known to the artist, and sometimes they are not, much to the delight and employment of Freudians everywhere.For example, did you know there’s lots of ears in Hamlet? There’s the poison-in-the-ear thing, of course, and characters are always eavesdropping on each other and exhorting each other to listen, but there’s also a lot of talk about ears (“in the porches of my ears”) and number of odd ear-based metaphors (“the whole ear of Denmark”, “like a mildewed ear”). Whether Shakespeare did this on purpose because he had some kind of ear fetish, whether the muse whispered it to him in his sleep (and through what orifice?), and whether any reader notices it—these are all beside the point. The recurrence of these themes and images creates a depth that can be felt even if it isn’t known, and endlessly explored if it is.2Humans are mortal, for now. This means all of our actions incur opportunity costs, and so the greater the cost paid to create a work of art, the thicker it can get. There’s no guarantee this will happen, of course, and that risk is part of the thrill.The Met Cloisters has these wooden altarpieces from the 1400s that draw your attention immediately, I think because the mind can subconsciously calculate the time it must have taken to carve them, and it sends a signal back to the eyes: important. You know that you are not just seeing a work of art, but the expenditure of a life.Here’s an even more haunting example. I once saw the magician duo Penn and Teller perform live, and at the end of the show, Penn told us he was going to swallow fire. As he dipped the torch in gasoline, he explained that what he was about to show us is not a trick. Magicians are always saying things like that, but in this case it’s true: there is no sleight of hand the protects the fire-eater from the flames. They get blisters and burns, the fuel drips down their esophagus and poisons them, they suck the hydrocarbons into their lungs and contract “fire-eater’s pneumonia”. To watch someone eat fire is to watch someone shorten their lifespan for your entertainment.“When you leave the theater tonight, you’re going to ask yourselves, ‘How did they do it?’”, Penn said as he lit the torch. “Instead, I’d like you to ask yourselves, ‘Why did they do it?’“ And then he reared his head back and swallowed the flame.The other way to understand thickness is to study its absence.Guys who work in bike shops like to joke about bicycle-shaped objects—sure, that mass-produced hunk of metal and plastic has a seat, pedals, wheels, and handlebars, but that doesn’t mean it’s a bike. When the materials are so cheap and the construction is so slapdash, it deserves another name entirely.This terminology comes in handy, because it turns out there are also movie-shaped objects and book-shaped objects, art-shaped objects and thought-shaped objects. Just because a series of pictures flickered across the screen and the credits followed, that doesn’t mean it was a movie. Just because it’s printed out and bound in cardboard, that doesn’t mean it’s a book. There is an additional essence that is necessary to turn something from the shape of a thing into the actual thing, and the difference between having and lacking that essence is the difference between a corpse and a person.This essence is what makes fiction worth reading in the first place, but it’s hard to capture in a paragraph, so let me show you some nonfiction instead, where you can spot the thinness in an instant. Here’s a passage from a self-help book that a friend sent me recently:You are built to perform under pressure and that is exactly what you will do. Reminding yourself of this changes the meaning of those signs of stress that might otherwise be seen as “symptoms” of a problem. In fact, research shows that simply reminding someone that their performance improves under pressure improves their actual performance by 33 percent (Jamieson et al., 2018).These sentences crumble immediately upon inspection. First of all, there’s something embarrassing and grating about getting generic encouragement from a book—you don’t know me! Maybe I am not “built to perform under pressure”! I might be a pathetic weakling who is destined to choke at the pivotal moment. What then?Plus, the facts here are brittle. I looked up the paper in question and could not find this “33 percent” number anywhere. Maybe it’s made up? And what is “performance”, anyway? Performance on anything? Surely not; the studies cited in the paper are mainly about taking multiple-choice tests.3 This is exactly the kind of finding that rises to prominence thanks to one small and flawed experiment, attracts a bunch of excited research, gets wildly overgeneralized under the handwavy phrase “studies show”, and then shrivels under a wave of debunkings and non-replications, such that after years of work, the whole thing ends with an embarrassed shrug. (Unsurprisingly, there is some evidence of publication bias for this “built to perform under pressure” effect.)Reading a book like this feels like wandering through a Potemkin village. Touch any of the ideas, and they tip over.In nonfiction, it might seem like the solution for puffery is pedantry, as if thickness comes from presenting every relevant fact in agonizing detail. But it doesn’t, just as thickness in fiction doesn’t come from describing every object in the room before you let the characters open their mouths. Instead, thickness comes from surfacing a few facts well, and in such a way that you realize the existence of entire universes of additional facts that could be known.For example, here’s a short passage from Jane Jacobs’ The Death and Life of Great American Cities:[City planners] operate on the premise that city people seek the sight of emptiness, obvious order and quiet. Nothing could be less true. People’s love of watching activity and other people is constantly evident in cities everywhere. This trait reaches an almost ludicrous extreme on upper Broadway in New York, where [...] benches have been placed behind big concrete buffers and on any day when the weather is even barely tolerable these benches are filled with people at block after block after block, watching the pedestrians who cross the mall in front of them, watching the traffic, watching the people on the busy sidewalks, watching each other.Jacobs notes that further north, near Columbia University, the streets are quieter, the pedestrians are more orderly, the traffic is calmer...and the benches are empty. “I have tried them and can see why,” Jacobs says. “No place could be more boring.”4There are a lot of threads here, so I’ll pick just one. Jacobs is pointing out a fact that millions of people observe every day, but almost none of them notice. Including me! I once lived on those boring blocks that Jacobs describes, and although I noticed something amiss—I would tell friends I lived in “the dead zone of Manhattan”—I never understood why. Nor do I think psychologists really have an answer for what motivates people to sit on benches and watch other humans go by. What drive is this satisfying?There is a danger, of course, in seeking and praising thickness, one that even I understood when I was a barely-sentient teenager. If you allow for the existence of secret treasures that can only be accessed with effort and analysis, then you empower the elitists and the snobs. “Buddy, don’t even talk to me until you’ve been in the cave!”But look around. The snobs are in full retreat. We have swung the pendulum so far toward poptimism, toward the blinkered idea that all art is equal because all humans are equal, toward the ethos that guilty pleasures are simply pleasures, that I’m not sure if we can ever swing it back.Erasing the line between the thick and the thin has left us defenseless against slop at the exact moment of its onslaught. Everyone can sense there’s something amiss with the prose that comes out of the machines, but we lack the language to talk about it, and so we’ve converged on the idea that slop simply means using too many em dashes, bullet points, and line breaks.No, what separates substance from slop is thickness. Slop holds no secrets; it signifies nothing. Under scrutiny, it evaporates. All it can offer is bottomlessness—sure, there’s nothing on, but at least there are infinite channels!That’s why I’m neither surprised nor dismayed when studies find that people prefer AI art to human art. Of course they do! In the short term, thinness prevails. When people are making snap judgments, they want pretty flowers, poems that rhyme, pleasing pablum, the simulacrum of thought.5 But none of these last. The real question is not “which of these things looks nicer when you look at them for two seconds?” but “which of these things will stand the test of time?” Which of them will people fly across the world to see? Which of them will drive people so mad they’ll major in the humanities?This kind of quality can only be proven by longevity. Which answers another question I had when I was scowling in the back of English class: why do we have to spend so much time reading old stuff? And the answer is: this is the only stuff that we can be sure is any good. Great works of art, like successful genes, convince humans to keep passing them on. If something has survived for centuries, then there’s probably something to it. We’re not still brewing Bronze Age beer and we’re not still sailing Bronze Age ships, but we are still telling Bronze Age stories, and this warrants our attention.Speaking of longevity, remember a few months ago, when everyone was Studio Ghibli-fying all the pictures in their camera roll? Well, why did they stop? Why are those millions of images gathering dust in a data center while people continue to watch actual Studio Ghibli films? Why is it that Suno can AI-generate you any kind of music you want, but if you go on the Suno Reddit, you’ll find a running joke that no one can stand anyone’s Suno music but their own—a quality that, I can’t help but mention, also applies to farts?The slop-acalypse that so many of us fear, when people will stop looking at anything made by humans and only look at things made by machines—why hasn’t that happened yet? Do the models need another million tokens? Are we still looking for the right prompts? Or could it be that we are attempting to mass-produce something that cannot be mass-produced?On the left: @clayohr on twitter. On the right: Francisco Goya.Regardless, people keep trying. About once a week, I get a pitch from some AI startup that wants to automate some part of my writing. The most recent one says it’s “built for credible thinkers who have a book’s worth of ideas but not the time it typically takes to write one”.I’m sorry, but if you’re building or using a tool like this, then you’ve got slop for brains. There is no such thing as having a “book’s worth of ideas” that are all ready to go except for the small matter of choosing the right words and putting them in the right order.I know exactly the feeling that these slop-trepeneurs are preying on, because I feel it all the time: I’ve got these thoughts in my head, and boy oh boy they’re good ones, all-timers, really, and it’s so annoying that I have to spend all this time making the words sound good, when the ideas behind the words are already so good!But this is an illusion. The ideas are not already good. They need to be thickened. I understand why it’s tempting to force a machine do the hard part for you, but it can’t, and the hard part is the only part worth doing anyway. Making something thick—that’s a lot of pressure! But remember: you were built to perform under pressure, and that’s just what you’ll do.3Also, those studies did not remind participants “that their performance improves under pressure”—they told participants that feeling anxious during a test doesn’t mean you will necessarily perform worse, and it might make you perform better.

What drive is this satisfying?There is a danger, of course, in seeking and praising thickness, one that even I understood when I was a barely-sentient teenager. If you allow for the existence of secret treasures that can only be accessed with effort and analysis, then you empower the elitists and the snobs. “Buddy, don’t even talk to me until you’ve been in the cave!”But look around. The snobs are in full retreat. We have swung the pendulum so far toward poptimism, toward the blinkered idea that all art is equal because all humans are equal, toward the ethos that guilty pleasures are simply pleasures, that I’m not sure if we can ever swing it back.Erasing the line between the thick and the thin has left us defenseless against slop at the exact moment of its onslaught. Everyone can sense there’s something amiss with the prose that comes out of the machines, but we lack the language to talk about it, and so we’ve converged on the idea that slop simply means using too many em dashes, bullet points, and line breaks.No, what separates substance from slop is thickness. Slop holds no secrets; it signifies nothing. Under scrutiny, it evaporates. All it can offer is bottomlessness—sure, there’s nothing on, but at least there are infinite channels!That’s why I’m neither surprised nor dismayed when studies find that people prefer AI art to human art. Of course they do! In the short term, thinness prevails. When people are making snap judgments, they want pretty flowers, poems that rhyme, pleasing pablum, the simulacrum of thought.5 But none of these last. The real question is not “which of these things looks nicer when you look at them for two seconds?” but “which of these things will stand the test of time?” Which of them will people fly across the world to see? Which of them will drive people so mad they’ll major in the humanities?This kind of quality can only be proven by longevity. Which answers another question I had when I was scowling in the back of English class: why do we have to spend so much time reading old stuff? And the answer is: this is the only stuff that we can be sure is any good. Great works of art, like successful genes, convince humans to keep passing them on. If something has survived for centuries, then there’s probably something to it. We’re not still brewing Bronze Age beer and we’re not still sailing Bronze Age ships, but we are still telling Bronze Age stories, and this warrants our attention.Speaking of longevity, remember a few months ago, when everyone was Studio Ghibli-fying all the pictures in their camera roll? Well, why did they stop? Why are those millions of images gathering dust in a data center while people continue to watch actual Studio Ghibli films? Why is it that Suno can AI-generate you any kind of music you want, but if you go on the Suno Reddit, you’ll find a running joke that no one can stand anyone’s Suno music but their own—a quality that, I can’t help but mention, also applies to farts?The slop-acalypse that so many of us fear, when people will stop looking at anything made by humans and only look at things made by machines—why hasn’t that happened yet? Do the models need another million tokens? Are we still looking for the right prompts? Or could it be that we are attempting to mass-produce something that cannot be mass-produced?On the left: @clayohr on twitter. On the right: Francisco Goya.Regardless, people keep trying. About once a week, I get a pitch from some AI startup that wants to automate some part of my writing. The most recent one says it’s “built for credible thinkers who have a book’s worth of ideas but not the time it typically takes to write one”.I’m sorry, but if you’re building or using a tool like this, then you’ve got slop for brains. There is no such thing as having a “book’s worth of ideas” that are all ready to go except for the small matter of choosing the right words and putting them in the right order.I know exactly the feeling that these slop-trepeneurs are preying on, because I feel it all the time: I’ve got these thoughts in my head, and boy oh boy they’re good ones, all-timers, really, and it’s so annoying that I have to spend all this time making the words sound good, when the ideas behind the words are already so good!But this is an illusion. The ideas are not already good. They need to be thickened. I understand why it’s tempting to force a machine do the hard part for you, but it can’t, and the hard part is the only part worth doing anyway. Making something thick—that’s a lot of pressure! But remember: you were built to perform under pressure, and that’s just what you’ll do.3Also, those studies did not remind participants “that their performance improves under pressure”—they told participants that feeling anxious during a test doesn’t mean you will necessarily perform worse, and it might make you perform better.

comments.author: hibikir
comments.textRawHtml:
The anecdote about the garden of earthly delights is going to be relatable even for art students. I've met art teachers that ended up "trapped" in Madrid by the Prado Museum: A green, American future Ph.D student that was heading to Greece to specialize in old greek art. But instead of flying straight there, they stopped at Madrid to see the Prado, and were never able to leave. Changed their direction immediately, and ended up teaching in Madrid, and retiring there, because one of the countless masterpieces in there stole their life plans away.

There's more famous museums, and it doesn't have the most popular paintings for non specialist, but it's just haymaker after haymaker, in every single room. And that's leaving the modern art to the Reina Sofia, a short walk away. (Although I guess keeping late Goya there is kind of cheating, as I'd argue he becomes a pioneer of modern art after the war starts)

Books might require quite a bit of work before you can tell they are eternal masterpieces. Seeing the depths of some forms of music might involve not-so-impressive efforts earlier, just to get to the good parts. The very best paintings in the world, in person, can stop people cold. Large format efforts that demand attention even when you don't consider every single small decision.

The Garden of Earthly Delights used to be stuck in a corner, at the edge of one of the wings of the Prado. As if "oh well, I guess it fits here, near all the medieval art". It counted as an ambush.
comments.textZhHtml:
即使对于艺术系的学生来说，关于尘世欢乐花园的轶事也会产生共鸣。我遇到过一些艺术老师，他们最终被普拉多博物馆“困”在马德里：一位年轻的美国未来博士生，正前往希腊专门研究古希腊艺术。但他们没有直接飞到那里，而是在马德里停留参观普拉多，然后就再也无法离开。他们立即改变了方向，最终在马德里教书，并在那里退休，因为那里无数的杰作之一夺走了他们的人生计划。

这里有更多著名的博物馆，而且没有非专业人士最受欢迎的画作，但每个房间里都有一个又一个的干草人。 现在，现代艺术就交给了距离酒店仅几步之遥的索非亚王后国家艺术中心 (Reina Sofia)。 （虽然我猜戈雅迟到有点作弊，因为我认为他在战争开始后成为现代艺术的先驱）

书籍可能需要大量的工作才能让你知道它们是永恒的杰作。要了解某些形式的音乐的深度，可能需要付出不那么令人印象深刻的努力，只是为了到达好的部分。世界上最好的画作，亲眼所见，可以让人不再感到寒冷。即使您不考虑每一个小决定，大型作品也需要引起注意。

人间乐园曾经被困在普拉多一侧机翼边缘的一个角落里。 就好像“哦，好吧，我想它适合这里，靠近所有中世纪艺术”。这也算是一次伏击吧。

children.author: jameshart
children.textRawHtml:
Totally. The right way to approach an art gallery is definitely just to walk round until something hits you.

Most astonishing time that happened to me was a wall-sized Rothko that just floored me, in a way I never would have expected a slab of color to.

Dali’s La Gare de Perpignan stopped me in my tracks too.

Rarely been as stunned by more famous works as when I got blindsided by something that leapt out and said ‘look’.
children.textZhHtml:
完全。进入美术馆的正确方式绝对是四处走走，直到有什么东西 点击数 你。

发生在我身上最令人惊讶的一次是一幅墙壁大小的罗斯科作品让我摔倒在地，这是我从未想到过的一块颜色。

大理的 佩皮尼昂站 我也停下了脚步。

很少有比我被突然跳出来说“看”的东西让我措手不及的著名作品更令我震惊的了。

children.author: encomiast
children.textRawHtml:
Possibly the best thing about Washington D.C. is that the National Gallery of Art (along with, I think, all the Smithsonian) is free. This means you just take a casual stroll through without any of the pressure of having spent a sizable sum like you might to visit a place like the Art Institute in Chicago. In Chicago a visit is an event, you need to see the Seurat, the Grant Wood, etc. You've spent money and you need make it count.

In D.C. you can literally walk in, go look at the big Joan Mitchell for 10 minutes and continue on your day. Or you can wander through a room you've never been interested in and find something and then go to lunch. Without the commitment to get everything done, you are suddenly free.

Good libraries (edit: even mediocre libraries) also have this quality.
children.textZhHtml:
华盛顿特区最好的事情可能是国家美术馆（我认为还有所有史密森尼博物馆）都是免费的。这意味着您只需随意漫步，而无需像参观芝加哥艺术学院这样的地方那样花费大量金钱。在芝加哥，参观是一件大事，你需要参观修拉、格兰特伍德等。你花了钱，你需要让它发挥作用。

在华盛顿特区，您实际上可以走进去，花 10 分钟看看伟大的琼·米切尔 (Joan Mitchell)，然后继续您的一天。或者你可以在一个你从来不感兴趣的房间里闲逛，找到一些东西，然后去吃午饭。没有完成所有事情的承诺，你突然就自由了。

好的图书馆（编辑：即使是平庸的图书馆）也具有这种品质。

children.author: bluGill
children.textRawHtml:
Many museums have a membership. For one price you can visit the museum any time you want. I strongly recommend everyone do this for all their local museums. It changes the experience when you don't feel bad about wasting the admission because you only have an hour. Particularly small local museums where spending all day isn't worth it, but if you have to pay admission you feel compelled to spend all day to get your money's worth.

Some of them also include reduced price admission to others of the same time. My local zoo isn't very big, but the membership means half price admission to a very good zoo just a couple hours away. My local science museum got me free admission to many other science museums and children's museums. My local historic farm got me into a lot of interesting historical sites. Be sure to understand what you get and take advantage of it on vacations.

I strongly recommend you get the version that lets you bring two guests. When my parents or some other friend from out of town comes to visit we have something interesting to show them (and if they are not having fun we can leave early).
children.textZhHtml:
许多博物馆都有会员资格。只需支付一笔费用，您就可以随时参观博物馆。我强烈建议每个人为他们当地的所有博物馆都这样做。 当你不因为只有一个小时而浪费门票而感到难过时，它会改变体验。特别小的当地博物馆，在那里花一整天是不值得的，但如果你必须支付入场费，你会觉得不得不花一整天才能让你的钱花得值。

其中一些博物馆还包括向其他同一时间的其他博物馆提供折扣门票。 我当地的动物园不是很大，但是会员资格意味着可以半价进入一个非常好的动物园，距离酒店只有几个小时的路程。我当地的科学博物馆让我可以免费参观许多其他科学博物馆和儿童博物馆。我当地历史悠久的农场让我参观了许多有趣的历史遗迹。请务必了解您将获得什么并在假期中充分利用它。

我强烈建议您购买可携带两位客人的版本。当我的父母或其他外地朋友来看望我们时，我们会向他们展示一些有趣的东西（如果他们不开心，我们可以提前离开）。

children.author: azath92
children.textRawHtml:
For those of us on the other side of the ditch: all museums in London are free. and I would echo the sentiment that it makes exploration of them less of a completionist activity to "get your monies worth" and more of an enjoyable forey into a rich space.

Its literally a paradigm shift.

Also almost all commercial art galleries are like this, obvs for other reasons. The gallery district (google art galleries then wander those streets, chelsea is the most established) in NYC is an amazing place to spend a day wandering around seeing amazing art. my uncle who teaches art introduced me to it and i try to spread the word.

Free art for any reason is amazing.
children.textZhHtml:
对于我们这些在沟渠另一边的人来说：伦敦的所有博物馆都是免费的。我同意这样的观点，即它使得对它们的探索不再是“让你的钱物有所值”的完成主义活动，而是更多地进入一个丰富的空间，这是一种令人愉快的尝试。

这实际上是一种范式转变。

此外，几乎所有商业艺术画廊都是这样的，出于其他原因。纽约的画廊区（谷歌艺术画廊然后在这些街道上漫步，切尔西是最古老的）是一个令人惊叹的地方，可以花一天的时间漫步欣赏令人惊叹的艺术。我教艺术的叔叔向我介绍了它，我尝试传播这个词。

任何原因的免费艺术都是令人惊叹的。

children.author: smattiso
children.textRawHtml:
I lived in DC for a couple of years and I felt exactly the same. I try and carry that same mentality to all museums now, paid or unpaid. No research, no expectations, wander around and let yourself be surprised, leave when you’re bored. It’s a lot of fun.

Although it is hard to do when you’ve paid 50 bucks for a ticket and you know there is “just one more” ultra-famous piece on the other side of the museum and when will I really be back in (Amsterdam, Paris, etc)?
children.textZhHtml:
我在华盛顿住了几年，我也有同样的感觉。我现在尝试将同样的心态带到所有博物馆，无论有偿还是无偿。没有研究，没有期望，四处闲逛，让自己感到惊讶，无聊时离开。这很有趣。

尽管这很难做到，因为你花了 50 美元买了一张门票，而且你知道博物馆的另一边“只剩下一件”超级著名的作品，而我什么时候才能真正回到（阿姆斯特丹、巴黎等）？

children.author: forgotmypasswor
children.textRawHtml: ^^ this. I was never an art person and then one day I felt like I was just punched in the face when it hit me. It's not like "I like this, it's interesting", it's like "Oh. That."
children.textZhHtml: ^^这个。我从来都不是一个艺术爱好者，有一天，当它击中我时，我感觉自己就像被打了一拳。这不是“我喜欢这个，这很有趣”，而是“哦。 那。”

children.textRawHtml: the punched in the face expression is strange here. I get it but I also presume that you have never been punched in the face much like you never connected (that's the word you are looking for, also a boxing term) with art.
children.textZhHtml: 这里被打孔的表情很奇怪。我明白了，但我也假设你从来没有被打过脸，就像你从未将艺术联系起来（这是你正在寻找的词，也是一个拳击术语）。

children.author: roarcher
children.textRawHtml: I presume you think having been punched in the face makes you special. I have too. It doesn't.
children.textZhHtml: 我猜你认为脸上被打一拳会让你变得特别。我也有。事实并非如此。

children.author: kstrauser
children.textRawHtml: You should also go apologize to your English teacher.
children.textZhHtml: 你也应该去向你的英语老师道歉。

children.author: pavel_lishin
children.textRawHtml: Perhaps more teachers should punch students in the face.
children.textZhHtml: 也许更多的老师应该打学生的脸。

children.author: the_af
children.textRawHtml: I wish I could do this. In general, in museums I always feel compelled to go through all the exhibits my time allows, when clearly some of them capture my attention and others are just filler. But I would feel guilty "wasting" my time with the piece that caught my attention.
children.textZhHtml: 我希望我能做到这一点。总的来说，在博物馆里，我总是觉得有必要把时间允许的所有展品都看完，显然其中一些展品吸引了我的注意力，而另一些则只是填充物。但我会因为在引起我注意的作品上“浪费”时间而感到内疚。

children.author: matthiasv
children.textRawHtml: I have the same feeling always, so for my upcoming trip to Amsterdam and a visit to the Rijksmuseum I vibed https://rijksmuseum.matze.lol to concentrate on something I _want_ to see.
children.textZhHtml: 我总是有同样的感觉，所以对于即将到来的阿姆斯特丹之旅和国家博物馆的参观，我感觉https://rijksmuseum.matze.lol专注于我想要看的东西。

children.author: dreamcompiler
children.textRawHtml:
The Rijksmuseum has a very nice shop too. It's a great place to wander and discover and you can browse it without paying museum admission.

https://www.rijksmuseum.nl/en/visit/practical-info/shop
children.textZhHtml:
国家博物馆也有一家非常好的商店。这是一个漫步和探索的好地方，您无需支付博物馆门票即可浏览。

https://www.rijksmuseum.nl/en/visit/practical-info/shop

children.author: cmdoptesc
children.textRawHtml: This is where a membership to the local museum comes in handy. Then there's no pressure to see all the exhibits because you could always come back next week.
children.textZhHtml: 这就是当地博物馆会员资格派上用场的地方。这样就没有压力去参观所有展品，因为您随时可以在下周回来。

children.author: baruz
children.textRawHtml:
But let’s not pretend that the plastic and painterly arts are so much more self-evidently “thick” than literature is. Despite their immediacy, these arts have their own conventions, motifs, and demands that must be understood to “find the treasure in the dark cave.”

I have tried to convince someone I know that an art museum merits more than a one-minute-per-painting, four minutes-max-per-room, pretty/not-pretty approach. She still does not understand why I linger over books or works of art, and I have not the wherewithal to lead her through the techniques, the conventions, or the history that makes this worthwhile for me.
children.textZhHtml:
但我们不要假装造型艺术和绘画艺术比文学更不言而喻的“厚重”。尽管这些艺术具有即时性，但它们有自己的惯例、主题和要求，必须理解这些惯例、主题和要求，才能“在黑暗的洞穴中找到宝藏”。

我试图说服我认识的人，艺术博物馆的价值不仅仅是每幅画一分钟、每个房间最多四分钟、漂亮/不漂亮的方法。她仍然不明白为什么我对书籍或艺术作品流连忘返，而且我没有足够的资金来引导她了解使这对我来说有价值的技术、惯例或历史。

children.author: Ntrails
children.textRawHtml:
> The very best paintings in the world, in person, can stop people cold.

I will always remember literally stopping mid stride to just stare at a Francis Bacon I'd seen in the corner of my eye in the Tate modern. Slightly later same day I am just staring at Monet lillies bewildered.

I gotta be honest, any time I go back I am disappointed because the same surprise and wonder have simple not been present. Idk
children.textZhHtml:
> 世界上最好的画作，亲眼所见，可以让人不再感到寒冷。

我永远记得我在泰特现代美术馆中停下来，盯着我在眼角余光中看到的弗朗西斯·培根。 当天晚些时候，我只是困惑地盯着莫奈百合。

我必须说实话，每次我回去我都会感到失望，因为同样的惊喜和惊奇没有出现。 我不知道

children.author: inglor_cz
children.textRawHtml:
I was in Prado and it felt overwhelming to me. Like trying to eat an entire cake. I think it must be taken in in measured doses.

Goya's museum in Zaragoza was the one I could take in during one visit.
children.textZhHtml:
我在普拉多，这对我来说是一种压倒性的感觉。就像试图吃掉整个蛋糕一样。我认为必须按一定剂量服用。

萨拉戈萨的戈雅博物馆是我一次可以参观的博物馆。

children.author: zmgsabst
children.textRawHtml:
I know almost nothing about music; can’t play a bit.

I can still distinctly remember the first time I heard Rachmaninoff performed in person — and the shock at the “brutal genius” of the art.

I think sometimes art just speaks to you.
children.textZhHtml:
我对音乐几乎一无所知；我对音乐几乎一无所知。有点玩不了。

我仍然清楚地记得第一次听到拉赫玛尼诺夫亲自表演时的情景，以及对艺术“残酷天才”的震惊。

我认为有时艺术只是对你说话。
